title: Would it be fun to watch an AI learn a game if it was built for spectators?
author: No_Bat_7448
selftext:
I’m prototyping a small game where the main player is an AI agent, not a human. The loop would be: it attempts a level, fails visibly, changes strategy. 

On top of this I’m working on a second model that’s live-commentating what’s going on and the view on the strategy. Something almost like a sports commentator or tv-host kind of commentary, that’s talking to the viewers about what the first model is trying.

Is this something that would even be interesting to watch? What would make this entertaining to watch long-term, and not get boring after a few min? What game formats do people think would be most interesting to try out? Some options I was thinking of:

* Platformer
* maze/escape room
* tactics game (think mafia or diplomacy or something)
* survival sandbox
* 4x strategy game
* Something else?

comments.author: Morph_Games
comments.body: It would be interesting to a few people, but the problem is that it takes millions of iterations to train it. The first group of iterations will be boring because it will be hopelessly clumsy. The last group will be boring because it will have mastered the game. The fun, the drama of bring a spectator lies in the unpredictable nature of a game/sport/etc.

replies.author: LogicalMelody
replies.body:
Yes, I’ve found I’m gravitating toward games where the AI is not generative, but tasked mainly with surfacing legibility on some underlying information it’s not allowed to touch. That architecture seems to help with long form stuff. As a simple example (not a game as such), I’ll feed Dwarf Fortress Legends to an LLM and ask it to explain the world to me to get a better sense of it.

For theory, reading Tynan Sylvester’s The Simulation Dream online, he’s right about the hairball problem but eliminating the game model and relying entirely on apophenia I think was the wrong move - 1) I can sense the relative lack of causal structure under RimWorld-storyteller events are largely injected randomness vs Dwarf Fortress’ richer causal substrate despite imo worse UI, and 2)both my whole mod stack and the official DLCs as I see it are trending toward trying to retrofit deeper causality onto the engine.

Design implication being I’d like to see rich simulated causality with AI as interpreter, not generator. Of course, this is naturally harder to write than just having the AI try to do everything, but in theory seems more stable - especially with research suggesting LLMs do better when highly specialized than when generic. Instead of trying to eliminate the hairball, use the LLM to surface meaningful parts of it. LLM as reader rather than writer.

Life by You is the only upcoming life sim I was interested in and it got canceled, which I personally think hurt the genre - it looked like it was trying to be causally interesting where most of the others feel more like they’re just Interior Decorating: The Game or Virtual Dollhouse to me.

Harrowlands I’m watching as the dev is inspired by Rimworld and trying to address certain weaknesses they perceive.

Simulation games in particular I think may be helped by LLM interpretation of a rich causal substrate. Even just an LLM news ticker riding on top of something like Victoria 3, or diary entries for Crusader Kings 3, I could see adding value.

Sorry about the length, wrote more than I expected here.
